\section[aparcar]{aparcar — to park}

\label{lesson:ES-C489-aparcar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to say goodbye, then the Spanish for to greet.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: aparcar}
\textbf{aparcar} — \textquotedblleft{}to park\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No se puede aparcar aquí.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{You cannot park here.}
\end{quote}

The verb behind \emph{el aparcamiento}, the car park. In Latin America people say \emph{estacionar}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aparcar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{aparcar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{aparcar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to say goodbye, then the Spanish for to greet, then say \emph{aparcar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does aparcar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To park\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el atasco]{el atasco — the traffic jam}

\label{lesson:ES-C489-atasco}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to greet, then the Spanish for to park.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el atasco}
\textbf{el atasco} — \textquotedblleft{}the traffic jam\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Hay un atasco a la entrada de la ciudad.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There is a traffic jam at the entrance to the city.}
\end{quote}

In much of Latin America people say \emph{el embotellamiento} or \emph{el tráfico}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for reading notices, forms and messages.
\end{grammarlens}
